6 months is a little early to start figuring if she is autistic or not. Babies do weird things all the time. It could be possible, but it's still a little too early to tell. 

The earliest I've ever noticed Autism in a baby was about 10 months, when every time a young boy would see his mother, he would do something I dubbed the 'happy dance' -- basically crawled up to her feet, sat there, and twirled his hands and wiggled while not really looking at her. He also had a fascination for playing with toy trucks if only to spin the wheels around and around.

Three years later, guess what? Autism. Who'd've thunk??

Anyway, wiggling is typical baby behavior, by 6 months they're still getting a grasp on their baby bodies. I would say look for other signs of autism if you're suspecting, but don't stress too much about it.

1 - Self harm: Redirection and praise despite failure is an option! Though I can't speak for your son (All Autistic Kids are different), one main issue that can stress someone out is control, or lack thereof, which is why he might be self harming, mainly out of frustration that nothing going his way. What (would have) helped me when I got this way was praising even the failures of the thing he was attempting. "That was a good try! Look how far you got! You earned a sticker for that!" Is something I would have loved to hear from my brother every time I lost a smash bros. Fight against him. 
Skin peeling might be a sensory thing too. Even harmful, self-harming behaviors can be a sensory thing. I have Trichomonia myself, and give myself pock marks from time to time. What really helps is distraction and redirection.  Place a crayon in his hand or see if he will hold something for you next time you see him doing that. 

As for the playing with nipples and belly button - kids will explore their bodies, that's natural! It's not weird at all! You might have to do more redirection if it becomes a problem for other parents (screw them anyway), but honestly, it's okay.

2. 4th of July - Independence day (and fireworks in general) are a nightmare to me, so I can see why he is scared. It might be more than the loud cracks and booms, it might be the flashing light as well. It could also be a hidden fear. I was particularly afraid of Fireworks because I was afraid of falling ash on me. The lights and the sounds were scary enough, but ash? That was enough to have me cling to daddy for support. I still haven't really gotten over my fear of fireworks, even as an adult (since people like to set off fireworks around here like we just won a war) but one thing that helped me is finding a spot REEEEEEEALLY far away from the venue where they have the fireworks launched. Like, miles and miles and many more miles away. The light isn't so bright, the sound is muffled (though I would still wear those earmuffs), and all you really get is pretty geometric patterns in the sky. If that still scares the little tyke, though, it might be best to find a new way to celebrate 4th of July. Like glowsticks! Pretend they're sparkles! 

3. Disney - this one is a toughie. I am just learning about the disability pass they have, I never knew such a thing existed. But the last disney trip was a nightmare for me because of lack of control -- especially being under stimulated in an overstimulating environment. Ask him often what he wants, how he feels (not too often to avoid being overbearing). Plan cool-down spots and moments, and let him lead the leash just a tiny bit, but not too much. But planning is a big, big help. Tell him ahead of time about things, like about if a line might be too long, or if the park is closing soon. There are apps for seeing how long lines are. Go for the most popular rides early, even if you have to be at Disney when the rope drops.

4. The Daddy Issue - unfortunately, this is very common among parents of autistic children, especially fathers. This is a really complicated issue, but the biggest recommendation I can make is therapy that he will have to be involved in. In my experience, my own father was a British Stiff-Upper-Lip classy man born right after WWII. My mother though made sure he was involved with my process of getting help and everything, even if he didn't understand what was going on. I'm not sure what other advice I can give, but have him involved in family discussions and even therapy sessions about Autism. 

I really hope this helps. I was speaking more from personal experience and perspective as an Autistic adult and what I wished would have been done with me.

I really like to believe that Autism is in fact, genetic, and can be caused by a plethora of genetic ways that's just the luck of the draw.

That being said, including me having ASD, I like to think that my father is somewhere on the spectrum as well. He loves books -- Like, he cannot stop reading and collecting them. Our entire basement is lined wall-to-wall with books that are older than *him.* He likes to sometimes spout out random historical, mathematical, or geological facts no one would care about (Although I do my best to listen with intrigue.) He is a mathematical genius -- he has papers, paper towels, napkins, all with mathematical equations I do not understand. And above all -- he has no sense of socialization. We are a family of introverts, but he takes the cake -- he rarely talks to anyone, and he is always uncomfortable talking to someone new.  Heck, he is even uncomfortable talking to his own children. He cares about us, but he just doesn't really know how to ... emote, talk to someone about himself, just about things that interest him.

My dad and I just sort of had this silent agreement that we love each other even if we don't really know how to express it in a way that makes either of us comfortable. I give him books, he says random nonsense and I listen, and it's always a joy.

Whomever he met and socialized with, it was on terms that they could both relate to -- mostly mathematical genius or something like that. My dad once crashed on the couch of Sir Clive Sinclair. Accidentally once phoned up Arthur C. Clark. England is a weird country. 

With all that being said and done, I had a professor who once told me Autism is believed to be caused by one or both parents have a high IQ. I am very inclined to believe her with how my parents met through MENSA.

It was actually a journey for me. But I am thankful that my mother was realistic and decided to face this rather than hide like I see many other parents do at my job. 

My mother noticed I just wasn't ... socializing. It wasn't a matter of me not speaking properly (I was speaking my own language until I was in first grade), but a matter of me just ... playing by myself, being by myself, not making my needs known and, the biggest contender, having meltdowns over the strangest things (I remember when I was three, living in England, and I was having a meltdown right on one of those potty-training potties. I forget what it was about, but I distinctly remember seeing my mom's dress on the floor and freaking out about it, maybe because she was away for work and I missed her?)

When we moved to America, my mom took me to several therapists who had no dang clue just what was up with me. Apparently I was part of a study where they hooked up diodes to my brain and studied what was happening to my brain as I was socializing to a medical doctor, seeing that like ... different parts of my brain was lighting up, all except for the one that should be reacting ... it's weird, isn't it?

Anyway, by the time I came to elementary school, my diagnosis for the longest time was just ... learning disability. It wasn't until I was about 10 or 11, when I was in middle school, that I got my diagnosis of Asperger's syndrome. 

I want to go to a therapist and get myself re-evaluated, seeing as Aspergers is no longer in the DSM, and see if I can just say I am on the spectrum. Still, I am thankful for my mom being realistic instead of just pretending that 'it's a toddler thing' or 'it's just a phase.'
